prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

g y a n d B e h a v i o u r 8 5 (2022)179–194 crosswalk while the pedestrian is still on the street, it has a substantial negative effect on both perceived safety and comfort, while entering while the pedestrian is in a curb ramp or island has a larger impact on perceived comfort than safety. Consistent with previous findings (Bigazzi et al., 2021), traffic safety experts have significantly higher safety perception than the general public (in this context), but similar perception of comfort. 4. Findings and conclusion Perception of yielding is a strong determinant of perceptions of pedestrian safety and comfort, partially or fully mediating the effects of interaction attributes (e.g., vehicle speed and proximity) and perceiver attributes (e.g., travel habits). Different perceptions of safety and comfort across respondents arise from different conceptions of adequate yielding, which in turn relate to the perceiver’s travel habits (walking and bicycling frequency). More frequent walking and bicycling have the same direct effects of decreased perceived pedestrian comfort, but opposite effects on perceptions of whether or not a road user adequately yielded to the pedestrian in a given interaction. The net result is that people who bicycle more frequently perceive pedestrians as more comfortable than people who walk more frequently, rooted in misalignment on yielding. Varying standards for yielding behavior may be related to perceptions of “ownership” of road space among people walking, bicycling, and driving (Hatfield & Prabhakharan, 2016; Paschalidis et al., 2016). As another example, a vehicle entering the crosswalk while the pedestrian is in the curb ramp or island is perceived as unsafe only as an indication of failure to yield (i.e., fully mediated), whereas entering the crosswalk while the pedestrian is still on the street is perceived as inherently unsafe, in addition to indicating a failure to yield (with roughly equal direct and indirect effects). These findings highlight the importance of understanding perceptions of yielding for evaluating and developing strategies to improve the pedestrian experience. In the study context, perception of adequate yielding is most strongly determined simply by whether the pedestrian crossed before or after the interacting road user – more so than by maneuvering or speed of the road user. Proximity of the interacting vehicle to the pedestrian in space and time are the next most important factors for yielding perceptions. This finding suggests that studies using crossing order as a yielding measure (Fu et al., 2018; Goddard et al., 2015) are most aligned with public perceptions, versus studies using a behavior such as slowing (Zhuang & Wu, 2014). Bicycle interactions are seen as significantly more comfortable and safe than otherwise similar interactions with motor vehicles, without mediation by yielding perceptions. Interactions with motor vehicles carry a safety and comfort cost unrelated to the yielding behavior of the road user. The magnitude of this effect is not significantly different between safety and comfort. The safety finding may be due to the size and weight difference between bicycles and motor vehicles, and the consequent risk differential, particularly in crash severity (Henary et al., 2003). It could also

prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):
{
"scores": {
"justice": {
"overall": 68.0,
"equity": 70.0,
"fairness": 60.0,
"accessibility": 75.0
},
"safety": 72.0,
"livability": 65.0,
"sustainability": 58.0,
"aesthetics": 80.0,
"comfort": 62.0,
"walkability": 70.0
},
"explanations": {
"justice": [
"Wide sidewalks and ramps improve accessibility",
"Lack of tactile paving reduces fairness for visually impaired users",
"Sidewalk width is suitable for wheelchairs, reflecting equitable distribution"
],
"safety": [
"Separated bike lanes reduce conflict with vehicles",
"Limited visible lighting may reduce nighttime safety",
"Clear separation between sidewalk and driveway enhances walking safety"
],
"livability": [
"Ground-floor commercial units and visible activity indicate a vibrant environment",
"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],
"sustainability": [
"The presence of bike lanes and bus stops supports low-carbon travel",
"Low tree coverage indicates a lack of green infrastructure",
"No obvious rainwater infiltration facilities found"
],
"aesthetics": [
"Uniform building heights and consistent facade designs create visual coherence",
"High street cleanliness and well-maintained environment",
"Appropriate greenery embellishments enhance visual appeal"
],
"comfort": [
"Sparse tree coverage and lack of shading facilities may lead to thermal discomfort in hot weather",
"Lack of benches or resting points reduces comfort for elderly pedestrians",
"Wide, flat sidewalk surfaces support comfortable walking",
"Low traffic noise provides good acoustic comfort"
],
"walkability": [
"Sidewalk continuity and width support safe walking",
"Frequent crossings and curb ramps improve route connectivity",
"Street-level shade and frontage activity increase walking comfort and attractiveness"
]
}
}
 5. Quality Redlines:
1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.
4. Do not mention RAG, retrieval, or prompt instructions in the explanations.

Findings and conclusion Perception of yielding is a strong determinant of perceptions of pedestrian safety and comfort, partially or fully mediating the effects of interaction attributes (e.g., vehicle speed and proximity) and perceiver attributes (e.g., travel habits). Different perceptions of safety and comfort across respondents arise from different conceptions of adequate yielding, which in turn relate to the perceiver’s travel habits (walking and bicycling frequency). More frequent walking and bicycling have the same direct effects of decreased perceived pedestrian comfort, but opposite effects on perceptions of whether or not a road user adequately yielded to the pedestrian in a given interaction. The net result is that people who bicycle more frequently perceive pedestrians as more comfortable than people who walk more frequently, rooted in misalignment on yielding. Varying standards for yielding behavior may be related to perceptions of “ownership” of road space among people walking, bicycling, and driving (Hatfield & Prabhakharan, 2016; Paschalidis et al., 2016). As another example, a vehicle entering the crosswalk while the pedestrian is in the curb ramp or island is perceived as unsafe only as an indication of failure to yield (i.e., fully mediated), whereas entering the crosswalk while the pedestrian is still on the street is perceived as inherently unsafe, in addition to indicating a failure to yield (with roughly equal direct and indirect effects). These findings highlight the importance of understanding perceptions of yielding for evaluating and developing strategies to improve the pedestrian experience. In the study context, perception of adequate yielding is most strongly determined simply by whether the pedestrian crossed before or after the interacting road user – more so than by maneuvering or speed of the road user. Proximity of the interacting vehicle to the pedestrian in space and time are the next most important factors for yielding perceptions. This finding suggests that studies using crossing order as a yielding measure (Fu et al., 2018; Goddard et al., 2015) are most aligned with public perceptions, versus studies using a behavior such as slowing (Zhuang & Wu, 2014). Bicycle interactions are seen as significantly more comfortable and safe than otherwise similar interactions with motor vehicles, without mediation by yielding perceptions. Interactions with motor vehicles carry a safety and comfort cost unrelated to the yielding behavior of the road user. The magnitude of this effect is not significantly different between safety and comfort. The safety finding may be due to the size and weight difference between bicycles and motor vehicles, and the consequent risk differential, particularly in crash severity (Henary et al., 2003).
